summary.verdict: Your buoyancy section is the best piece of first-principles engineering writing on any of the four hardware pages, and nearly all of it checks out: 3.51 cm³ per millimetre of draft, 1 mm per 3.5 g, the kink at 79.4 g and the 92.6 g solid print all agree with Table 1. What the page does not have is a plate doing its job, and a reader who could build one. Both exist in the project: our Plants page carries four named outside people who handled the hydroponics setup, a box volume, an air stone and a printed board in use, and none of it is on this page.
strengths: The buoyancy arithmetic holds together. The load line, the 1 mm per 3.5 g rule, the kink at 79.4 g and the 92.6 g solid print all follow from Table 1, and the 117.50 by 92.50 by 25.08 mm envelope matches a 3.18 mm slab on 21.91 mm pontoons to 0.01 mm.

Five numbered requirements, each with the sentence that answers it. Two of them, one standard printer and nothing to glue, are about whether anyone else can build it. No Best Hardware winner writes requirements this cleanly.
The page says what it has not done, in the results block where a judge sees it first: the printed plate was not weighed, the print settings are partial, the files are not attached.
Figure 3 is turned into a tool. You give the density the arithmetic rests on, then tell the reader to weigh the plate, find that mass along the bottom and read the freeboard up the side.
The 180 g case from an earlier draft is kept and fenced off in the same paragraph, with the number that proves it does not belong to this plate.
priorities: Bring the outside users onto the page. Our Plants page names Prof. Cheng Mei-Chun (27 March and 28 August, with two setups left with her to watch over a longer period), Dr. Kyle (17 June, topping up concentrates what is left behind), Prof. Chen Wen-liang (20 June, a recirculating system and an auto-filling reservoir) and the farm visit of 11 August that changed the CAD the same day. The second ballot question asks whether you tested with users and learned from them, and this page answers nothing.

Attach the four STLs and finish the print settings. Every number on the page is measured off files the reader cannot have, and layer height, wall count and orientation are the three settings a reprint needs most. Your own photometer page has the block to copy.

Report the plate in water. The printed version was never weighed, and the page never says whether it floated, at what freeboard, or with seedlings in it. Our Plants page says the box running now is prototype 4 with the foam board replaced by a 3D printed board, so something of this design is already in use.

Check the sealed chamber numbers. A pentagon 6.99 mm wide and 20.32 mm deep, 114.33 mm long, comes to about 14.8 cm³, so the pair is about 29.7 cm³ and not 42.27 cm³. The 42.27 figure is the one your other numbers support, so the length is the one to check.
Say what the plate floats in. Container, medium volume, the minimum depth that clears a 15.9 mm draft, and the air stone your own hero caption implies. Then fill the Cost column or delete it.

ballot.question: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?
ballot.note: The lab problem is concrete and three improvised setups are named, but the page never says which of our own assays the plate serves, and the sentence that there was no commercial equipment to buy sits on the Plants page instead of here.

ballot.question: Did the team conduct user testing and learn from user feedback?
ballot.note: Nobody outside the hardware group appears anywhere on the page, although our Plants page records four named people and the design changes that followed each of them.

ballot.question: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?
ballot.where: Design Evolution has the printed version; the results block says the load line is unchecked
ballot.note: Nothing reports the plate floating, carrying seedlings or holding air. The page is honest about it, and a judge still has no proof of concept to score.

ballot.question: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?
ballot.note: The geometry is documented better than on any winner page, and the files are not attached, the cost cells are empty, the printer is unnamed, and there is no assembly order and no reservoir.

skeleton.gap: Four of the five winner slots are here, in the winners' order, and the design and build slot is deeper than theirs. The missing slot is Demonstration, which four of the five winners place last or second to last: one run of the device doing the job it was built for. Full DBTL Cycles sits exactly where that slot would go and sends the reader to another page.

extras: Thirteen is written as a word and as a digit for the same count: "thirteen Arabidopsis seedlings" in the summary, "Carry 13 Arabidopsis seedlings" in R2, "13 bores" in the results, "Print thirteen" in section 9. Pick one form for the plate's own counts and keep digits for dimensions.
"four STLs printed on a normal FDM machine" in 2.1, against "a standard FDM machine" in the summary and R4. One phrase, used everywhere.

Table 2's row "Nothing: the middle of the plate is flat slab, open underneath" says what Figure 4's caption and its image description already say. Keep the table row, which is where a builder looks, and cut the clause from the caption.

Table 1's first three rows have no figure in the Assembled column and the note below does not say why. Add one clause: above a freeboard of 12.2 mm nothing of the handles or holders is under the water.
The bill of materials and the print settings are both inside folds. They are the two things the fourth ballot question asks for, and the no-accordion rule in Jacquelyn's edit already covers them.

notes.anchor: A printed plate that floats on the medium, so thirteen Arabidopsis seedlings sit at one depth
notes.title: The first sentence does three jobs
notes.body: This names the device, the number it carries and the problem it removes, in one line, with no adjectives in it. A hardware judge reads this before anything else. Aachen's winning page takes three sentences to do the same work.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen names the need, the device and who it is for in its opening. Yours is shorter and holds the same three things.
notes.ballot: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: two chambers inside the pontoons, 42.27 cm³ between them, with no foam block and nothing strapped underneath
notes.title: The foam block is denied four times
notes.body: No foam block and nothing strapped underneath appears here, in R3, in the first paragraph of section 4, and again in Figure 4's second pin. Keep it once, in R3, where it is the requirement. Better still, say once why foam lost: our Plants page has the reason, that the foam board "is easy to break and became softened after it stayed in the water for a long time".
notes.after: two chambers inside the pontoons, 42.27 cm³ between them.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen keeps the rejected option on the page and says in one clause why it lost. That is what the foam deserves here.

notes.anchor: which gives the plate a load line: it sits about 1 mm lower for each 3.5 g it carries
notes.title: The load line has two slopes
notes.body: The 3.5 g per millimetre figure only holds while the slab is clear of the water. Past 79.4 g the whole slab displaces and it takes about 10 g to sink it a millimetre, which Figure 3's caption says and the summary does not. A judge who only reads the summary will carry away the wrong number.
notes.after: which gives the plate a load line: up to 79.4 g it sits about 1 mm lower for each 3.5 g it carries, and about 1 mm for each 10 g after that.

notes.anchor: In PLA on 25 June, with washers on four corner poles to trim the freeboard
notes.title: One date in three forms
notes.body: This row says 25 June, Figure 6's caption says 25 June 2026, and step 02 of Design Evolution says "started 6/25". A reader outside the United States has to guess at 6/25, and the year is missing from two of the three. Use one form with the year.
notes.after: In PLA on 25 June 2026, with washers on four corner poles to trim the freeboard

notes.anchor: The printed plate was not weighed, so the load line is unchecked against a real part
notes.title: The gap is stated where it counts
notes.body: You name what was not done and what it costs the claim, in one line, in the results block instead of a future work list at the bottom. TUDarmstadt does the same with its OD sensor and still won. Keep this row exactly as it is.
notes.excerpt_note: Built, but neither tested nor integrated in time, admitted in the same paragraph as the part itself.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: One STL per printed part Four files Plate, two handles and the seed holder
notes.title: This row promises a download
notes.body: The status word is "Four files", and section 9 says "The files are not yet attached to this page". A judge reading only the results block will believe the STLs are there and will mark the reproduction question accordingly. Say the true state in the row, or attach the files and keep the row.
notes.after: One STL per printed part · Drawn, not attached · Plate, two handles and the seed holder: 74.72 cm³ across sixteen pieces
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: a piece of foam cut to size, a mesh taped over a container, or a fixed plate sitting above a reservoir
notes.title: The need is built from real benches
notes.body: Three things labs actually do, named in order, and then the cost of all three in the next sentence. That is how TUDarmstadt opens: what the work needs, what is used now, and what is wrong with it. The reader knows the problem before any dimension appears.
notes.excerpt_note: Four moves in one paragraph, ending on the gap the project fills. Yours is the same shape without the prices.
notes.ballot: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: None of it is repeatable between labs, or even between runs in the same lab.
notes.title: Two sentences are on the wrong page
notes.body: The ballot asks for a need in synthetic biology, so a judge wants to know what you would otherwise buy and which experiment this serves. Our Plants page has the first one already: "We had assumed that a hydroponic rig was something you had to buy, but since there was no specialized commercial equipment, we decided to build our own version." Add that sentence and one naming the assay the plate carries.
notes.after: None of it is repeatable between labs, or even between runs in the same lab. There is no commercial rig to buy for this, so we built our own, and it carries the seedlings for our [name] sets.
notes.excerpt_note: Evry justifies a second device in one sentence, from the first device's need and a budget. One sentence is enough.
notes.ballot: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: Our plate floats on the medium, so the seedlings stay at the same depth no matter how much liquid is left.
notes.title: The answer arrives before the question
notes.body: This paragraph gives the solution, and 2.2 then spends three paragraphs explaining the problem it solves. Move it after 2.2, so the purpose reads as problem, then diagnosis, then answer. The two headings can stay as they are.
notes.after: End 2.1 on the repeatability problem, and open 2.2's close with this paragraph: "Our plate floats on the medium, so the seedlings stay at the same depth however much liquid is left. The whole thing is four STLs, so another lab can run the same geometry we did."

notes.anchor: Same depth, same spacing, same conditions, whoever is running it.
notes.title: Same conditions claims too much
notes.body: The plate holds the depth and the spacing. It does not hold the volume of medium or its strength, and both change through a run as the plants drink and the water evaporates. Our Plants page treats that as a real variable, so a judge who grows plants will stop here. Claim the two things you hold.
notes.after: Same depth, same spacing, whoever is running it.
notes.excerpt_note: TUDarmstadt states what its machine gives and then what it cannot give, in the same breath. The bounded claim is the stronger one.

notes.anchor: It also does not stay where you put it. The plants drink and the medium evaporates
notes.title: The old design fails for a reason
notes.body: The mechanism comes first, then what it costs the person running the experiment, then the decision: "That is what we set out to remove." You never call the fixed plate a bad idea, you show why it could not hold. This is Evry's move and it is the best paragraph in your Purpose section.
notes.excerpt_note: A plan described in full, then killed by one number and one mechanism. The reader is left understanding the fix.
notes.ballot: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: Over a fixed plate it has to stay in a narrow window: too high and the platform floods, too low and the roots lose contact
notes.title: The caption repeats the paragraph
notes.body: The body says this two paragraphs above, in almost the same words. Our editor's rule for these pages is that when the prose and the thing next to it say the same thing, one of them goes. Leave the caption with what the figure shows and the fact that it is schematic.
notes.after: The level falls through a run. Over a fixed plate it has to stay in a narrow window; a floating plate falls with the level, so the roots stay at the same depth. Schematic, not to scale.

notes.anchor: Hold root depth constant for the whole run, with no manual topping up.
notes.title: This requirement has a named source
notes.body: Our Plants page says where it came from: on 17 June Dr. Kyle pointed out that topping up evaporated medium concentrates the salts and sugars left behind, and from then on the team stopped topping up. A requirement with a date and a person behind it is worth far more to this ballot than a requirement on its own. Prof. Chen Wen-liang's auto-filling reservoir, suggested on 20 June and not built, is the alternative you rejected.
notes.after: Hold root depth constant for the whole run, with no manual topping up. Dr. Kyle pointed out on 17 June that topping up concentrates the salts and sugars left behind, so topping up stopped being an option.
notes.excerpt_note: UBC names the people, says what their expertise is, and says what their words bought. Dates and names cost you nothing here.
notes.ballot: Did the team conduct user testing and learn from user feedback?

notes.anchor: The plate floats, so the seedlings stay at the same depth however much liquid is left. Sections 2.2 and 4.
notes.title: Three times for one sentence
notes.body: This is the summary's first sentence and 2.1's first sentence again. In a requirement, the only new thing here is the cross-reference, so let the line be short.
notes.after: The plate floats. Sections 2.2 and 4.

notes.anchor: Carry 13 Arabidopsis seedlings.
notes.title: Where thirteen comes from
notes.body: Thirteen is the number this whole page is built around and nothing here says where it came from. Our Plants page has the answer: after the farm visit on 11 August you redesigned the float plate, and "The current design has thirteen planting positions." One clause closes it, and it also explains the 21.59 mm pitch.
notes.after: Carry 13 Arabidopsis seedlings, the number the plate settled on after the farm visit in August.
notes.ballot: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: Assemble with no adhesives and no fasteners.
notes.title: Two requirements about other people
notes.body: R4 and R5 are not about what the plate does, they are about whether a stranger can build it. No winner in the Best Hardware set writes a requirement like that, and these two are the reason your geometry is reproducible at all. Say in one clause that this is why they are here.
notes.excerpt_note: Evry makes documentation a design constraint that drove component choice. Your R4 and R5 are the same idea, written as requirements.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: The plate floats on a sealed air volume built into its own frame.
notes.title: Sealed depends on the print
notes.body: The whole design rests on two printed chambers holding air, and a printed wall can leak. The page never says a chamber was checked. Hold one under water for a few minutes, watch for bubbles, and write down the time and what you saw. That is an afternoon, and it is the cheapest answer this page can give to the functionality question.
notes.excerpt_note: Volume, inoculum, strain, time, and the one observation that settles it. A leak test reads the same way: how long under water, and whether anything came out.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: The teardrop is the sealed chamber inside each pontoon: a box section 6.99 mm wide
notes.title: The table already holds these numbers
notes.body: This sentence and the Sealed chambers row of Table 2 give the same four dimensions in nearly the same words. Keep the numbers in the table, where a builder will look for them, and let the prose say what the shape is and why it is that shape.
notes.after: The teardrop is the sealed chamber inside each pontoon, a pentagon in section with its lower sides chamfered to a point (Figure 5, Table 2). The two chambers hold 42.27 cm³ of sealed air between them.

notes.anchor: Sizing them is a displacement problem.
notes.title: Open the section with this line
notes.body: This is the sentence that tells a reader what section 4 is doing, and it arrives third, after two paragraphs of answers. Put it first, then the solution, then the dimensions. The section is strong enough that it should not make the reader wait to find out what question is being asked.
notes.after: Open section 4 with: "Sizing the flotation is a displacement problem. The plate has to displace its own mass plus the seedlings plus any water it takes on, while sitting at the freeboard that puts the roots in the medium and the crowns above it." Then the sealed air volume and the teardrop.

notes.anchor: it has to do that while sitting at the freeboard that puts the roots in the medium and the crowns above it
notes.title: Say what freeboard the plants need
notes.body: The section computes the freeboard at every mass and never says which freeboard the seedlings need, or where 9.2 mm came from. Cornell's habit is to put the requirement next to the capability, which is what turns a specification into evidence. One sentence will do it.
notes.after: it has to do that while sitting at the freeboard the seedlings need: roots at least [number] mm into the medium and crowns [number] mm clear of it, which is the 9.2 mm the plate is drawn at.
notes.excerpt_note: 37 klux delivered against 3,000 lux required, and 20% brightness used. The requirement next to the capability is what makes the number mean something.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: The waterline is drawn 6.0 mm under the slab, a freeboard of 9.2 mm
notes.title: The caption gives away the paragraph
notes.body: This caption states the drawn freeboard and the 54.2 cm³ displacement before the paragraph below derives them and before point 1 of Figure 3 lists them. Let the caption say what the figure shows, and leave the numbers to the text that explains them.
notes.after: A displacement problem. Section A to A of the CAD, afloat at the freeboard the plate is drawn at. The plate settles where its mass equals the mass of medium it displaces.

notes.anchor: Measured off the CAD, the displacement at each waterline gives
notes.title: Put this plate on its own chart
notes.body: Figure 3 runs from 0 to about 120 g and never says what this plate weighs, so a reader cannot find it on the chart you built for them. The slicer gives the printed mass at 15% gyroid in seconds, and thirteen seedlings can go on a balance. Mark that point and the figure answers the question a reader actually has.
notes.after: Add one marked point and one clause: "At 15% gyroid the sixteen parts come to [number] g, so a plate with thirteen seedlings on it sits at about [number] mm of freeboard."
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: In water at 1.00 g/cm³ every cubic centimetre displaced floats a gram
notes.title: Your medium is not plain water
notes.body: The load line assumes 1.00 g/cm³, and the plate floats in half strength MS medium with sucrose in it, which is a little denser. The difference is small and a judge will want to see you say so. One clause is enough.
notes.after: In water at 1.00 g/cm³ every cubic centimetre displaced floats a gram, and we take the medium as water, which is within [number]% of that
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: so weigh the assembled plate with its seedlings, find that mass along the bottom, and read the freeboard up the side
notes.title: The chart comes with instructions
notes.body: You give the density the arithmetic rests on, then tell the reader how to use the figure, in the second person, in one sentence. That turns a graph into something another lab can actually use on its own plate. This is the sentence to copy onto the other three hardware pages.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen writes to the stranger who might build the thing: your sample, your experiments. Your sentence does it with a procedure instead of a promise.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: The slab’s underside meets the water at 79.4 g and 3.2 mm. From here the whole slab displaces, so each gram sinks it less.
notes.title: The bend in the curve is explained
notes.body: You say where the load line changes slope and why, in one sentence, so a reader can read the rest of the chart without you. The arithmetic holds: from 79.4 g to 111.9 g over 3.2 mm is 10.2 g per millimetre, which is the figure in Figure 3's caption.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: Solid PLA: printed solid, the sixteen parts would weigh 92.6 g at most, and float with 1.9 mm of freeboard.
notes.title: Name the density behind this
notes.body: The 92.6 g only follows if the reader knows which PLA density you used. At 1.24 g/cm³ your 74.72 cm³ comes to 92.7 g, and 1.9 mm of freeboard is right on your own curve, so the line is correct and unverifiable as written. Add the density and the check takes one line.
notes.after: Solid PLA: printed solid at 1.24 g/cm³, the sixteen parts would weigh 92.6 g, and float with 1.9 mm of freeboard.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: Freeboard is the slab top above the water; draft, the pontoon bottoms below it.
notes.title: Draft sets a minimum depth
notes.body: If the pontoons reach 15.9 mm below the water at the drawn freeboard, the medium has to be deeper than that or the plate grounds out, and the level falls all run by design. Our Plants page says the boxes hold 250 to 500 mL. A builder needs the minimum depth and how far the level can fall before the plate touches bottom.
notes.after: Freeboard is the slab top above the water; draft, the pontoon bottoms below it. The plate needs at least [number] mm of medium under it, so a box at [number] mL can lose [number] mm before the pontoons touch bottom.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: computed exactly from the STLs
notes.title: An STL is not exact
notes.body: An STL is a triangle mesh, so every curve in it is faceted: the 10.39 mm bores and the 3.81 mm corner radii are polygons in the file. A volume read off the mesh is close to the CAD solid and not exact. The page also swaps between "measured off the STLs", "Measured off the CAD" and this phrase for the same work, so a judge cannot tell which model the numbers come from. Pick one source word and drop "exactly".
notes.after: computed from the STLs the parts print from
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: needed about 0.65 cubic inches (about 10.7 cm³) of extra volume each
notes.title: One unit system on the page
notes.body: Everything else here is millimetres and cubic centimetres. The conversion is right, 0.65 in³ is 10.65 cm³, and it is the only hint that the model is drawn in inches, which is also why your dimensions land on 10.16 mm, 1.59 mm, 25.40 mm and 114.33 mm. Give this one in cm³ and say once that the CAD is in inches, so nobody reads two decimal places as a tolerance.
notes.after: needed about 10.7 cm³ of extra volume each
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: That mass is not this plate: 180 g is well past the 111.9 g at which the plate measured here goes under
notes.title: An old number, fenced off
notes.body: You keep a worked case from the drafts, say in the next clause that it does not belong to this plate, and give the number that proves it. Then you say what the load line actually stands on. This is the best paragraph on the page, and it is the move to copy wherever an old number survives on the other three hardware pages.
notes.excerpt_note: TUDarmstadt bounds its own claim in the paragraph that makes it. Yours bounds a number from an older draft the same way.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: The four corner poles on the first floating version were the safety margin on this.
notes.title: The poles are told four times
notes.body: The ballast poles appear in this fold, in Figure 4's fourth pin, in step 02 of Design Evolution and again in step 03. Tell the story once, in step 02, where the version that had them lives, and leave a pointer here. The fold's own title says it holds two subjects.
notes.after: Leave one line here: "The first floating version carried washers on four corner poles as the margin on this (section 6)." Move the rest to step 02.

notes.anchor: Teardrop cross-section on the pontoon tubes, which prints without support and sheds the overhang cleanly.
notes.title: A shape chosen for the printer
notes.body: The geometry is justified by one manufacturing consequence, in the same sentence that names it. That is how Cornell writes its material choices, and it is the reason your "no supports needed" line is believable later.
notes.excerpt_note: Materials listed, then justified by one consequence: the whole assembly can be autoclaved. One consequence per choice is enough.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: so there is nothing to glue or strap on and nothing to come loose in the medium
notes.title: Say how the plate is cleaned
notes.body: This part sits in warm medium for days with roots on it, and contamination is the main problem our Plants page reports from the hydroponic boxes. A reader rebuilding this needs to know what you wash it with, and that PLA softens well below autoclave temperature. One clause here, and one line in section 8.
notes.after: so there is nothing to glue or strap on and nothing to come loose in the medium. The plate is cleaned with [method] between runs; PLA will not take an autoclave.
notes.excerpt_note: Cornell draws the line between the instrument and the biology at sterility, and says which parts can be autoclaved and which cannot.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: Clip-in handles, so the plate lifts out of the reservoir without anyone touching the seedlings.
notes.title: The reservoir is never described
notes.body: The reservoir is mentioned three times on this page and described nowhere: no container, no volume, no depth, no air. Our Plants page has all of it, including 250 to 500 mL per box, a tank kept dark, medium changed every two to three days and "continuously aerated with air stones", which is what your own opening animation means by aerated water. Without those four facts nobody can set this up.
notes.after: Add one line in section 8: "The plate floats in a [volume] mL box, [dimensions], kept dark and aerated with an air stone, with the medium changed every two to three days."
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: One inside each pontoon, 114.33 mm long overall: a box section 6.99 mm wide
notes.title: The chamber numbers do not multiply
notes.body: A pentagon 6.99 mm wide and 20.32 mm deep with its lower sides chamfered to a point has an area of about 130 mm², and 114.33 mm of it is about 14.8 cm³, so the pair is about 29.7 cm³ and not 42.27 cm³. The 42.27 figure is the one your other numbers support: 105.9 cm³ of submerged shell minus 63.60 cm³ of printed plate is 42.3 cm³. So the length is the number to check, and 42.27 cm³ at that cross-section wants about 163 mm, which is close to the pontoon's full run including the hooked ends.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: 117.0 cm³ with the handles and seed holders as well (Table 1)
notes.title: Table one does not say that
notes.body: Table 1's assembled figure with the slab top awash is 111.9 cm³, not 117.0, so the pointer sends a reader to a number that is not there. Both figures look right to me for different waterlines: 117.0 is every part wholly under water (105.9 plus 5.52 plus 5.59), while at freeboard 0 the handles still stand 26.51 mm up in the air. Say which waterline each belongs to.
notes.after: 75.9 cm³ up to the underside of the slab; 105.9 cm³ with the whole plate submerged; 117.0 cm³ with the handles and seed holders submerged as well, which is past the last row of Table 1
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: We ran the displacement calculation again every time the design changed (section 4)
notes.title: Section four said this already
notes.body: Section 4 has this sentence with its reason attached, which is the better place for it. What this step needs is what the poles did and when they came off.
notes.after: How it changed: the poles were the safety margin on the buoyancy, and later iterations tuned the volume closely enough that they came off.

notes.anchor: Smaller footprint, clip-in handles, and buoyancy tuned closely enough that the ballast poles were no longer doing anything.
notes.title: Give step three the line the others have
notes.body: Steps 01 and 02 each end with why the design changed. Step 03 stops, so a reader cannot tell what drove the current shape or when. Our Plants page has it: the farm visit on 11 August, where you looked at the underside of a commercial growing channel, discussed the design on the spot and "started modifying our own CAD model that same day", which is also where the thirteen positions came from.
notes.after: Smaller footprint, clip-in handles, and buoyancy tuned closely enough that the ballast poles came off. Why it changed: a commercial hydroponic farm on 11 August showed us how their float boards are carried, and we changed the CAD the same day.
notes.excerpt_note: UBC introduces each new feature by the earlier experience that forced it. One clause is what makes an iteration read as learning.
notes.ballot: Did the team conduct user testing and learn from user feedback?

notes.anchor: It was never put on a balance (section 4).
notes.title: It was never weighed; was it floated
notes.body: This says what was not done, and the reader's next question is whether the printed plate ever went into water, at what freeboard, and whether the washers were needed. Our Plants page says the box running now is prototype 4 with the foam board replaced by a 3D printed one, so a printed board is in use with plants on it. Say which printed version that is and what it did.
notes.after: It was never put on a balance (section 4). Afloat in [volume] mL of medium it sat at about [number] mm of freeboard, with [number] washers on each pole.
notes.excerpt_note: Two sentences turn a picture into evidence, because the check was designed. A ruler against a floating plate is the same kind of cheap.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: DBTL cycles on the Plants DBTL page
notes.title: Name the page as the menu names it
notes.body: There is no page called Plants DBTL. The menu has Plants, and that page's sections are Abstract, Outcomes, Overview and design, Results, Dry lab collaborations, Outreach and Future work, with no DBTL heading in it. This line is also not a link. Name the page and the section a reader should open, and link it.
notes.after: The full cycles are on the Plants page, under [section name].
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: Stage by stage, this is what this page already holds.
notes.title: The T is missing from DBTL
notes.body: The band is labelled DBTL and the list under it has Design, Build and Learn. Test is the one stage this page has nothing in, and leaving it out hides that where the rest of the page is honest about it. Our editor's rule for these pages is one short paragraph per stage, naming what has not been tested yet, so write the Test paragraph and let it say the plate was never weighed and never reported afloat.
notes.after: Stage by stage, this is what this page holds, and what it does not. Test: nothing yet. The printed plate has not been weighed and no freeboard has been read off a real part.
notes.excerpt_note: The admission sits with the thing it concerns, not in a future work list at the end.
notes.ballot: Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?

notes.anchor: Buoyancy sizing, the CAD and its drawings
notes.title: Four stages, four short paragraphs
notes.body: These three chips carry four or five words each, where the other hardware pages give a short paragraph per stage. A judge reading the band learns nothing it could not guess. Write Design, Build, Test and Learn as one short paragraph each, with the dates you already have.
notes.after: Design: the buoyancy sizing, the CAD and its drawings, recomputed at every change. Build: the first floating version, printed in PLA on 25 June 2026 with washers on four corner poles.

notes.anchor: What each version changed, and why
notes.title: Four outside people are missing here
notes.body: The Learn stage is where the ballot's second question would be answered, and this page names nobody. Our Plants page has four: Prof. Cheng Mei-Chun at NTU on 27 March and 28 August, with two setups left with her to watch over a longer period; Dr. Kyle on 17 June on topping up; Prof. Chen Wen-liang on 20 June on a recirculating system and an auto-filling reservoir; and the farm director on 11 August. Three of the five Best Hardware winners score lower than that, and leaving someone else running your device off the page gives it away.
notes.after: Learn: what each version changed, and why. Prof. Cheng Mei-Chun's group grows Arabidopsis on foam boards, and two of our boxes were left with her in August to watch. Dr. Kyle's point about topping up on 17 June became R1. Prof. Chen Wen-liang asked for a recirculating system on 20 June, which we have not built.
notes.excerpt_note: Both name the people, where it happened, and the technical remarks that came back. Neither winner managed to leave the device with a user, which you did.
notes.ballot: Did the team conduct user testing and learn from user feedback?

notes.anchor: One floating plate, two clip-in handles and thirteen seed holders, drawn apart from the CAD.
notes.title: An exploded view is not an assembly
notes.body: A reader with your four files still has to work out the order, which way up each part goes, and what it floats in. Four numbered steps cover it, and you have all four facts already. TUDarmstadt gives seven steps with a photograph each and it is the best documented page in the winner set.
notes.after: Add under this figure: "1 Print the four parts (8.2). 2 Press the thirteen holders into the bores from above. 3 Clip a handle onto each end of the slab, foot under the slab, grip up. 4 Float the plate in a box holding at least [number] mL, kept dark and aerated."
notes.excerpt_note: Cornell names the manual and itemises what is in it: assembly, operation, precautions, differences between variants.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: Volume is the solid volume of one part in the CAD, not the filament a print uses
notes.title: An empty column is worse than a sentence
notes.body: The table has a Cost header with nothing under any of the four rows, and then a sentence saying no cost is recorded. Either price it or delete the column and keep the sentence. You also tell the reader this is not the filament figure and then never give the filament figure, which is the one a builder needs; the slicer prints grams per plate.
notes.after: Volume is the solid volume of one part in the CAD. The slicer puts the whole set at [number] g of PLA, about [number] of a spool, which is [price].
notes.excerpt_note: Cornell's parts list carries unit price, quantity and line total, and then a caveat saying which variant the prices belong to. A priced table with a caveat beats an empty column.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: A standard FDM printer
notes.title: Name the printer you used
notes.body: The Printer row answers a builder's question with a claim about a class of machine. You printed one on 25 June, so name that machine and its nozzle here, and keep the standard FDM claim for R4 where it belongs.
notes.after: [Printer name], [nozzle] mm nozzle. Any standard FDM machine should print these parts.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: Layer height, wall count and print orientation are not recorded.
notes.title: Our photometer page has the format
notes.body: This is the page whose entire output is printed parts, and these three are the settings a reprint needs most. Wall count matters twice here, because the sealed chambers hold air only if their walls fuse. Your photometer page records printer, nozzle, plate, profile, layer height, infill, supports and filament; copy that block. While you are in there, say what the 15% gyroid fills, since the chamber inside each pontoon is air and the plastic around it is only 1.59 mm thick.
notes.after: Replace the line with the slicer's own rows: layer height [number] mm, [number] walls, printed [orientation], 15% gyroid in the plastic around the chambers.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: The plate, the handles and the holder all print in PLA (8.2).
notes.title: The third time for PLA
notes.body: The bill of materials says all four parts print in PLA and the print settings row says PLA, both on the screen above this one. The cross-reference alone does the job.
notes.after: The four printed parts, one STL each, rendered here from their own files (8.2).

notes.anchor: The files are not yet attached to this page.
notes.title: Four files, four links
notes.body: This one sentence costs the page the fourth ballot question. The files exist, because every number on the page is measured off them, and the rendered views beside this line come from them. Attach them here and give each one its size, as your photometer page does with its eight STLs.
notes.excerpt_note: Evry promises replication and never links a file, and the casebook calls it the commonest reproduction failure in the winner set. You are one upload away from not repeating it.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

notes.anchor: The slab, both pontoons and their sealed chambers, as one print.
notes.title: Each file says what it holds
notes.body: A reader who downloads four files knows which is which, what is inside each print and how big it is before opening anything. That is unusual: two winners link files with no description at all. Keep this list as it is and hang the downloads off it.
notes.excerpt_note: Cornell itemises what is in its manual in one sentence. Your four descriptions do the same job for four files.
notes.ballot: Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?
